entry.title: Comparing Patient Experiences with SDM-Q-9, CollaboRATE, and iSHAREpatient in Routine Oncology Care: A Patient-Centred Evaluation
entry.summary:
Patient Education and Counseling · 2026-11-01 · group authors: Anniek van Hienen, Anshu Ankolekar, Simone Mingels, Rianne Fijten
Objective Shared decision-making (SDM) is preferred in oncology, yet routine evaluation in clinical practice remains challenging. This study aimed to compare patients’experiences of completing three widely used patient-reported SDM questionnaires (SDM-Q-9, CollaboRATE, and iSHAREpatient) under the same routine oncology-care conditions. Methods This multiple-methods study included 159 patients attending radiotherapy intake consultations at a large academic radiotherapy centre. Immediately after consultation, participants were randomised to complete one of three SDM questionnaires. Quantitative measures comprised the After-Scenario-Questionnaire (ASQ), (perceived ease, time investment, and support needs) completion time and clarification questions. Qualitative methods comprised think-aloud sessions followed by codebook thematic analysis. Results ASQ scores did not differ significantly between questionnaires for perceived ease, time investment, or support (p > 0.05 ). CollaboRATE was fastest to complete (mean 52 seconds), followed by SDM-Q-9 (2:17 minutes) and iSHAREpatient (3:46 minutes) (p < 0.001). iSHAREpatient generated more clarification questions than SDM-Q-9 and CollaboRATE. Qualitative findings revealed differences in patients’ completion experiences. SDM-Q-9 and iSHAREpatient prompted reflection on consultations and treatment decisions; while this may support engagement, it may also increase cognitive effort . When patients did not perceive a meaningful treatment choice, SDM-related questions were sometimes experienced as irrelevant, reflecting a mismatch between questionnaire assumptions and patients’ decision-making experiences. Conclusion SDM-Q-9 showed a favourable balance between comprehensiveness and ease of completion. CollaboRATE was the fastest to complete and may be particularly useful in time-constrained settings, whereas iSHAREpatient provided a more detailed assessment of the decision-making process. Practice implications Questionnaire selection should consider decision context, patient burden and the measurement purpose: SDM-Q-9 may be particularly useful when meaningful treatment choices are discussed, whereas CollaboRATE may be more suitable in time-constrained or predetermined decision settings, and iSHAREpatient when a more detailed exploration of the decision-making process is desired.

entry.title: Building a Radiation Therapy Ontology
entry.summary:
CEUR Workshop Proceedings · 2024-10-25 · group authors: Andre Dekker
This poster reports on our ongoing work to develop a Radiation Therapy Ontology (RTO) designed according to OBO Foundry principles.This work aims to produce an ontology describing the domain of radiation therapy concerned primarily with the processes and equipment used to deliver therapeutic radiation in a clinical setting.Currently in radiation oncology, around 3% of patients are enrolled in clinical trials.Major hurdles to involving more patients include the work required to identify potential enrollees, collecting the data, and transforming data to meet protocol requirements.Axiomatically rich ontologies are uniquely positioned to serve as a bridge between the precision needed in clinical trials and the reality of electronic health records.This work is also motivated by the recent push for standardization in radiation oncology, and the realization that progress in clinical practice requires better access to clinical data.RTO aims to be useful in bridging institutional and clinical practice differences.The proliferation of standard terminologies can be at odds with each other and with existing data labels.Currently, nearly all patient data are in relational databases with no overall uniformity with respect to schemas, tables, column names and value sets.The structure of these databases is most often controlled by the vendors, and in those cases where institutions tailor the names and variables, there are no fixed standards.The upshot is that one must expect that for nearly every application, some transformation of the data will be needed.

entry.title: Early Prediction of In-Hospital ICU Mortality Using Innovative First-Day Data: A Review
entry.summary:
arXiv · 2025-05-18 · group authors: Xuanhe Hou
The intensive care unit (ICU) manages critically ill patients, many of whom face a high risk of mortality. Early and accurate prediction of in-hospital mortality within the first 24 hours of ICU admission is crucial for timely clinical interventions, resource optimization, and improved patient outcomes. Traditional scoring systems, while useful, often have limitations in predictive accuracy and adaptability. Objective: This review aims to systematically evaluate and benchmark innovative methodologies that leverage data available within the first day of ICU admission for predicting in-hospital mortality. We focus on advancements in machine learning, novel biomarker applications, and the integration of diverse data types.

entry.title: A 3D transfer learning approach for identifying multiple simultaneous errors during radiotherapy
entry.summary:
Physics in Medicine and Biology · 2024-01-17 · group authors: Cecile Wolfs
Objective. Deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), can take full dose comparison images as input and have shown promising results for error identification during treatment. Clinically, complex scenarios should be considered, with the risk of multiple anatomical and/or mechanical errors occurring simultaneously during treatment. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the capability of CNN-based error identification in this more complex scenario.Approach. For 40 lung cancer patients, clinically realistic ranges of combinations of various treatment errors within treatment plans and/or computed tomography (CT) images were simulated. Modified CT images and treatment plans were used to predict 2580 3D dose distributions, which were compared to dose distributions without errors using various gamma analysis criteria and relative dose difference as dose comparison methods. A 3D CNN capable of multilabel classification was trained to identify treatment errors at two classification levels, using dose comparison volumes as input: Level 1 (main error type, e.g. anatomical change, mechanical error) and Level 2 (error subtype, e.g. tumor regression, patient rotation). For training the CNNs, a transfer learning approach was employed. An ensemble model was also evaluated, which consisted of three separate CNNs each taking a region of interest of the dose comparison volume as input. Model performance was evaluated by calculating sample F1-scores for training and validation sets.Main results. The model had high F1-scores for Level 1 classification, but performance for Level 2 was lower, and overfitting became more apparent. Using relative dose difference instead of gamma volumes as input improved performance for Level 2 classification, whereas using an ensemble model additionally reduced overfitting. The models obtained F1-scores of 0.86 and 0.62 on an independent test set for Level 1 and Level 2, respectively.Significance. This study shows that it is possible to identify multiple errors occurring simultaneously in 3D dose verification data.

entry.title: Participatieve en theoretische ontwikkeling van samen beslisseninterventies in de radiotherapie
entry.summary:
Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research) · 2026-11-17 · group authors: Anniek van Hienen, Rianne Fijten
Purpose: To describe the patient partnered development and of a multilevel shared decision making (SDM) programme for radiotherapy using Intervention Mapping. Methods: We applied Intervention Mapping combined with participatory design across six iterative steps: (1) assessing SDM needs through mixed methods; (2) specifying outcomes for patients, clinicians, the clinic and referrers; (3) selecting behaviour change techniques and translating them into practical applications; (4) integrating components into a coherent programme; (5) planning implementation strategies; and (6) designing an evaluation plan. A working group of seven (former) radiotherapy patients collaborated throughout, with ongoing input from clinical stakeholders. Results: The needs assessment revealed a gap between desired and experienced SDM. We defined two behavioural goals for patients and radiation oncologists—applying all SDM steps and empowering patients to accept the invitation to share decisions and three environmental goals. Sub-behaviours were formulated and linked to cognitive determinants like knowledge and attitude. These informed practical applications, including a pre-intake value-clarification tool, physician trainings and adaptations in patient-facing information materials. Effectiveness is currently evaluated through consultation observations and patient surveys. Patient partners contributed insights during >10 sessions, reviewed behavioural goals, prioritised determinants, and co-developed patient-oriented interventions. Conclusion: Intervention Mapping offers a structured approach for designing SDM interventions from a behavioural perspective. Patient participation is useful and feasible by including patients in a planning team. We recommend this approach for future SDM research, particularly when aiming for long-term patient involvement.

entry.title: Investigating Context in How Clinicians Make Sense of AI: Qualitative Interview Study
entry.summary:
JMIR Human Factors · 2026-11-13 · group authors: Simone Mingels, Hannah Piehl, Rianne Fijten
Background: AI-driven clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly being introduced to enhance clinical decision-making, yet their adoption in health care remains limited. Research has examined technical, organizational, and contextual barriers to adoption, but less attention has been paid to how knowledge, values, and responsibility around AI-CDSS are constructed and negotiated in practice. Objective: This study examines how clinicians and AI experts make sense of AI-CDSS by reanalyzing qualitative interview data through a feminist and constructivist science and technology studies (STS) perspective. Whereas the original study examined informational needs, this reanalysis asks how participants construct relevant knowledge, evaluate the value of AI-CDSS, and negotiate appropriate use and responsibility in clinical practice. Methods: The authors conducted a reanalysis of semistructured interviews held in 2024 with clinicians (n=8) and AI experts (n=8) in the Netherlands. The original study focused on informational needs for AI-CDSS. For this analysis, a deductive coding framework based on European Commission guidelines for trustworthy AI was first applied, and the material was then inductively reorganized into 5 empirical themes. Subsequently, feminist and constructivist STS concepts were used as sensitizing concepts in an abductive analysis, and these concepts were brought into dialogue with the empirical themes to examine the sociotechnical relations underlying participants' accounts. Results: Situated knowledge shows that the informational needs of clinicians are not universal but relate to their roles and specific clinical contexts, with understanding oriented less toward technical transparency than toward actionable guidance, relevance, and integration into decision-making. Standpoint theory illuminates differences between stakeholder priorities: clinicians emphasize information on how to use and act on AI outputs within existing workflows, whereas AI experts focus more on providing technical characteristics and performance metrics. Tinkering captures how clinicians experiment with AI systems in practice to develop situated, lay forms of expertise. Situated value highlights that perceptions of an AI-CDSS's worth are relational, with clinicians valuing novel, context-sensitive insights and developers prioritizing performance metrics. Finally, response-ability reveals how trust and accountability are largely delegated to institutional structures, while clinicians report limited legal, organizational, and structural support to respond meaningfully to uncertainty or errors when using AI-CDSS. Conclusions: Reanalyzing the same interview material through an abductive STS approach makes sociotechnical dimensions visible that were not the focus of the original analysis. Rather than treating informational requirements as universal or adoption as primarily a matter of technical performance and communication, the findings show how knowledge, value, and responsibility are constituted through situated professional practices and institutional arrangements. Processes and considerations regarding how clinicians make sense of AI-CDSS are not universal but are shaped by social, cultural, and institutional contexts. This analytical perspective underscores the need for context-sensitive, multistakeholder strategies to support meaningful and responsible AI adoption in clinical practice.

entry.title: Development, validation, and pilot-testing of a comprehensive patient-reported EORTC custom questionnaire for monitoring real-world tyrosine kinase toxicity in chronic myeloid leukemia
entry.summary:
Supportive Care in Cancer · 2026-11-12 · group authors: Rianne Fijten, Andre Dekker
PURPOSE: In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), treatment choices between tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are guided by efficacy and tolerability, yet no instrument adequately captures tolerability from the patient perspective. As a result, TKI choice may not comprehensively take into account the prevalence and severity of what patients' experience. We therefore developed, validated, and pilot-tested a new custom questionnaire to capture real-world patients' experiences, and explored pilot data. METHODS: A mixed-methods study was conducted, following COREQ and STROBE guidelines. Development started with CML-specific items from existing instruments, followed by semi-structured sessions with purposefully sampled patients, and convenience-sampled professionals, focused on comprehensibility, comprehensiveness, relevance, acceptability, workflow, and graphics. Based on qualitative analyses, items were substituted or added from the EORTC Item library. Psychometric quantitative evaluation assessed filter question validity, redundancy, reliability, measurement error, responsiveness, scale construction, and symptom severity differences in pilot data and meta-analyses. RESULTS: A new EORTC custom questionnaire was developed, covering 50 symptoms. Seven of those symptoms are covered by scales consisting of multiple items, with a Cronbach's alpha ≥ 0.73 for each of those scales. Psychometric properties further showed fair-to-excellent reliability and positive agreement between time points ranging from 45 to 93% in test-retest, while responsiveness was indicated for half of symptoms. Twenty-four generic filter questions are available for computer adaptive testing, an option preferred by 87% of patients. For 23 issues, no existing EORTC item was available; these need to be added later. Pilot data showed that the severity of symptoms, as reported by patients, differed significantly between the three most common TKIs in a third of symptoms. These significant differences ranged from 5 to 30%. The highest difference was for swelling of the eyes or face, which was reported 30% more severe in patients on imatinib, compared to patients on nilotinib, when adjusted for age, gender, years since diagnosis, years on current treatment, and TKI-dosage. We could not adjust for comorbidity or comedication. CONCLUSION: We developed and validated an EORTC custom questionnaire and workflow to monitor 50 CML patient-reported toxicity symptoms in clinical care. Sexuality problems are excluded from pre-existing instruments, yet pilot data revealed these are prevalent and severe from patients' perspective. One-third of evaluated symptoms varied in severity by type of TKI treatment, independent from age, gender, years since diagnosis, years on current treatment, and TKI-dosage. These findings can tentatively inform shared decision-making, when switching TKIs due to intolerability.

entry.title: A Blueprint for National and International Healthcare Data Ecosystems: Learning From Building STRONG ‐ AYA
entry.summary:
Learning Health Systems · 2026-11-08 · group authors: Leonard Wee
Introduction: Healthcare systems aim for continuous improvement to ensure excellent clinical outcomes, including optimized quality of life. This relies on accurate data and evaluation patient-centered as well as biomedical outcomes. This data increasingly arises from real-world data (RWD). We are using this data across a multi-national European consortium, to create a Learning Healthcare System, improve care, policy, and ultimately patients' outcomes. Methods: STRONG-AYA is an interdisciplinary community, led from the Netherlands Cancer Institute, working across frequent consensus meetings, surveys, questionnaire design, data collection, synthesis and privacy-preserving federated analysis (in Vantage6), to ethically study and apply clinical and patient-centered outcomes data to learn about healthcare systems for Adolescents and Young Adults (AYAs) diagnosed with cancer when aged 15-39. The young people themselves are at the heart of our decision-making, and we work to make our data analyses transparent. Results: A harmonized 'Core Outcome Set' was agreed with all stakeholders. We developed definitions and data science methodological approaches, aligned with Learning Healthcare System practices. We have built AYA cancer data ecosystems, at local, national and European levels, to combine informatics with lived experience, clinical and scientific interpretation, based upon initial 'use cases' of the mental health consequences and cancer survival rates. We are applying those insights in real time individual clinical care, individual patient education and support as well as service level metrics. Conclusions: The Strong-AYA Learning Healthcare System for AYA-onset cancer can empower discovery by health researchers, digital innovation, and innovative insights for patients, clinicians, managers and policymakers who aim for transformational improvements in the quality and outcomes of current clinical practice though the development of a Learning Healthcare System in AYA-onset cancer care. Sustainability is our next major challenge.

entry.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Semi-automated Personal Health Data Curation and Reuse for Myocardial Infarction
entry.summary:
European Heart Journal - Digital Health · 2026-11-05 · group authors: Wenjie Liang, Rutger van Mierlo, Cecile Wolfs, Aiara Lobo Gomes, Andre Dekker, Petros Kalendralis
Background and Aims Digital applications have high potential in myocardial infarction management. This study aims to harmonize personal health data using a workflow driven by an Artificial Intelligence-assisted virtual assistant prototype, then reuse the data to facilitate the creation of standardized patient summaries and risk assessment. Methods The required configurations for data documentation and curation were developed to drive the workflow execution. With consent and data transfer agreements, data of patients with myocardial infarction were extracted from multi-source medical records, structured and ingested into the workflow. After transformation, personal health data were mapped into concrete clinical concepts connected with specific relationships defined by the reference ontology, forming source health knowledge graphs as the basic structure of personal health knowledge graphs. Then the constructed graphs were validated by using Shapes Constraint Language-based constraints, triggering the human-in-the-loop process to enhance data quality. Information queries were conducted for data reuse. Results 38 out of 45 planned patients were recruited with a signed informed consent. Thirty patients finalized the study. Overall successful data ingestion rate is approximately 83%. The average data quality score is 95.45/100. Constructed personal health knowledge graphs can be reused to represent medical information as an international patient summary and evaluate individual risk of future cardiovascular events by calculating the Second Manifestations of Arterial Disease risk score. Conclusion Our proposed workflow is feasible for semi-automated personal health data curation and secondary use. It provides a potential solution to enhance medical data interoperability, thereby facilitating risk assessment in cardiovascular diseases.

entry.title: Stakeholder perspectives on implementing geographic information systems for leprosy elimination in Pakistan: A qualitative study
entry.summary:
PLoS ONE · 2026-11-05 · group authors: Johan van Soest
INTRODUCTION: Leprosy remains a pressing global health concern, with Pakistan among countries still facing missed and delayed diagnosis. By highlighting elevated risk areas, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are a cost-effective solution to improve leprosy case detection by guiding targeted interventions to high-risk areas. This study's purpose was to investigate the perceived GIS implementation facilitators and barriers, to support targeted interventions and advance the Zero Leprosy strategy. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twelve stakeholders, including local field staff, program managers, and international experts. Thematic analysis was guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory (DOI) to identify facilitators and barriers concerned with GIS implementation for leprosy. RESULTS: Key facilitators included an integrated multi-disease and pilot-based rollout approach, capacity building activities, offline-capable tools, and improved visibility to drive motivation. Barriers included the limited local capacity in complex GIS data analysis, hybrid digital-manual workflows, historical data lacking GPS, and ensuring feedback and ownership for staff members. CONCLUSION: GIS implementation is not only dependent on individual readiness, but also on broader external and organizational facilitators and constraints. This necessitates holistic implementation strategies that recognize the interconnectedness of different parts of the system. Internal capacity building is paramount to address statistical complexity and to build trust, ownership, and independence. As the world moves closer to achieving Zero Leprosy, integrating GIS within a multi-disease approach will be critical to making sustainable progress in combatting neglected tropical diseases.

entry.title: Deep learning model predicts recurrence in thymic epithelial tumours: a multicentre study
entry.summary:
Mediastinum · 2026-10-01 · group authors: Rianne Fijten
BACKGROUND: Thymic epithelial tumours (TETs) are the most common primary neoplasms of the anterior mediastinum. Despite complete surgical resection (R0), a significant proportion of patients experience recurrence, highlighting the need for improved prognostic stratification. Morphological patterns recognised in clinical practice may have prognostic value, and this study applies deep learning (DL) to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole slide images (WSIs) to predict recurrence in TETs, assisting pathologists in risk assessment and enabling precise treatment planning. METHODS: A multicentre cohort of resected TET patients with complete (R0) resection and no distant metastasis was assembled from Erasmus Medical Centre (EMC), Maastricht University Medical Centre (MUMC+) and the TCGA public dataset, with an external validation cohort from Hospices Civils de Lyon (HCL). WSIs were annotated in QuPath and sampled at 20× magnification into 512×512 patches. HCL WSIs, stained with haematoxylin-eosin saffron, underwent Vahadane normalisation to harmonise staining across centres. Patch embeddings from a pretrained Phikon encoder were aggregated through a multi-instance learning for patient level recurrence prediction, using stratified three-fold cross-validation. GradCAM applied to the most contributing patches generated heatmaps of the areas of highest model activation. RESULTS: Recurrence occurred in 19 of 298 patients (6.4%) internally and 5 of 95 (5.3%) externally. The model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.85, a balanced accuracy (BAcc) of 0.71, and sensitivity of 79% internally. Performance was preserved externally (AUC 0.70, BAcc 0.62, sensitivity 80%) despite domain shift. In true positive cases, heatmaps consistently localised to tumour tissue adjacent to fibrous septa, capsular structures and vascular interfaces, with additional focal activation in areas of increased cellular heterogeneity in tumours lacking prominent separation. CONCLUSIONS: The DL model can identify TET patients at risk of recurrence following R0 resection and demonstrates generalisability across institutions with differing tissue preparation protocols. Heatmaps corresponded to septal, capsular and perivascular structures, sites classically associated with tumour invasion and recurrence risk in TETs, suggesting the model may capture histological correlates of invasive behaviour. Future work will focus on larger datasets, multimodal architectures integrating clinical and imaging data, and further external validation.

entry.title: Mixed histology is a prognostic factor for recurrence in completely resected thymic epithelial tumours: a multicentre retrospective study
entry.summary:
Mediastinum · 2026-10-01 · group authors: Rianne Fijten
BACKGROUND: The recurrence of thymic epithelial tumours (TETs) following complete resection remains unpredictable. While the Masaoka-Koga staging system and WHO subtype classification are useful for clinical decision-making, no externally validated prognostic model exists to inform risk-adapted follow-up. Tumours with composite histological patterns, such as B2+B3 or B3+TC, are usually classified by their dominant subtype, potentially underestimating their aggressiveness. This study aimed to determine whether a machine learning (ML) model using these routine pathological variables could predict recurrence in completely resected TETs and whether including mixed histology would improve risk stratification. METHODS: Clinical data were collected from four centres (EMC, UMC+, TCGA and HCL). Patients with R1/R2 resection or stage IV disease were excluded. An internal development cohort (EMC (n=89), UMC+ (n=102), TCGA (n=116) and a geographically independent external validation cohort (HCL, n=95) were defined. A binary variable was introduced to identify tumours presenting two or more WHO subtypes. Six ML algorithms were evaluated and explainability was ensured through SHAP-based feature attribution. RESULTS: Patients with mixed histology had a recurrence rate of 18.5% (5/27) compared to 5.1% (14/277) in single-subtype cases (χ²=5.49, P=0.02). Among the six algorithms, Random Forest achieved the most consistent performance, with a balanced accuracy (BAcc) of 0.73 and Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.73 on the internal development cohort and a BAcc of 0.73, AUC of 0.72 and sensitivity of 0.80 on the external validation cohort. Ablation analysis confirmed the independent contribution of the mixed subtype indicator, as its removal reduced specificity by 0.03 and 0.08 in the internal and external cohorts respectively. SHAP analysis revealed that Masaoka-Koga stage IIb and subtype B2 had the highest feature importance, partly reflecting their prevalence in the dataset. Importantly, the overall pattern was consistent with established clinical knowledge, that aggressive subtypes and higher stages driving recurrence and indolent subtypes acting as protective, suggesting the model learned authentic clinicopathological relationships. CONCLUSIONS: We developed an interpretable, externally validated model built on routine pathology data achieved clinically meaningful recurrence prediction in completely resected TETs. Our results support formal recognition of mixed histological subtypes as an independent risk factor and their inclusion in pathology may improve postoperative risk stratification.

entry.title: Brain state locks silent memories in a trained fly connectome
entry.summary:
bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Xuanhe Hou
SUMMARY Complete connectomes now exist for insect nervous systems, but whether a fixed wiring diagram can learn, and what its memories consist of, is unknown. Here, we trained a spiking model of the whole male Drosophila central nervous system, 167,106 neurons with fixed wiring, to plan moves and to remember a visual cue. Spikes write the cue into neuronal adaptation, which holds it silently until the next input reads it out. Cells that hold the trace are enriched for transcripts of a calcium-activated potassium channel in fly cell atlases. The learned readout recalls the trace only in the brain state of learning: the same trace evokes a different response at another delay, and a disease-like loss of potassium current rewrites the trace and changes how it is read. Learning in the new state is spared. Memory failure can arise from a change of state rather than a loss of storage. HIGHLIGHTS A fixed whole-fly connectome learns to plan and to remember a visual cue The cue is held silently in neuronal adaptation and read out by the next input Recall works only in the brain state of learning, at writing and at reading A disease-like lesion rewrites the trace, while learning in the new state is spared IN BRIEF Wang et al. train a spiking model of the whole male fly nervous system to plan and to remember. It holds a visual cue silently in neuronal adaptation and recalls it only in the brain state of learning, so a disease-like lesion removes recall while new learning is spared.

entry.title: The limits of privacy enhancement in healthcare federated learning: a ELSA perspective in the EU context
entry.summary:
Frontiers in Big Data · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Marine Jacquemin
Federated Learning (FL) usage is steadily increasing in healthcare. Offering an attractive alternative to centralized data processing, FL is often promoted as a privacy-enhancing technology (PET) because it keeps patient-level data local, exchanging only aggregated data or model updates. As such, it is frequently presented as a means of addressing the ethical, legal and societal challenges associated with the use of sensitive health data. This framing has contributed to growing policy interest in FL within initiatives such as the European Health Data Space (EHDS). This paper examines FL from an ethical, legal and societal (ELSA) perspective in the EU context, focusing on its interaction with the European data protection framework and contemporary debates on health data governance. First, it analyzes the interaction between FL architectures and the General Data Protection regulation (GDPR), showing that questions of controllership, joint responsibility, and identifiability persist despite decentralization, particularly in complex multi-institutional settings. Second, it argues that privacy-centric approaches to health data governance remain ethically insufficient because harmful inferences, discrimination, and collective harms may arise even when data remains formally anonymous. The dominant focus on reidentification risk thus reflects a narrow and individualistic conception of privacy that is poorly adapted to the contemporary data landscape of the EU. It fails to capture broader forms of harm, including group-level discrimination, inferential profiling, and structural power asymmetries. The paper concludes that, despite its framing as a PET, the use of FL alone is not sufficient to guarantee appropriate health data protection. Indeed, FL should also be approached as a distributed data-processing paradigm in which risks and benefits depend on implementation choices, institutional arrangements, and regulatory interpretation. Accordingly, FL should be situated within broader questions of data governance, including how access, accountability, and collaboration are structured and distributed across institutions.

entry.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability
entry.summary:
European Radiology · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Sander Puts, Martijn Nobel
OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests. RESULTS: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). CONCLUSION: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

entry.title: IEKB: a comprehensive knowledge base for inner ear genetics integrating curated associations, cochlear interactions, Bayesian candidate prioritisation, explainable dark-gene support relations, and a scientific entity network
entry.summary:
bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) · 2026-04-09 · group authors: Xuanhe Hou
Inner-ear genetics has expanded rapidly, yet the supporting evidence remains dispersed across a vast literature and across resources that typically emphasise loci, variants, or expression data rather than integrated biological interpretation. Here we present the Inner Ear Knowledge Base (IEKB; https://earkb.org), an open database that unifies curated associations, cochlear interaction evidence, candidate prioritisation, explainable support relations, and network exploration for inner-ear research. IEKB was built with an automated agent-assisted curation workflow that combines schema-constrained literature extraction, continuous human monitoring, and final expert review by inner-ear genetics researchers. By systematically analysing 250,696 PubMed-indexed records retrieved across 16,563 screened genes, IEKB curates 6,051 gene–phenotype–disease associations from 2,494 genes across 43 phenotype categories and 4,102 cochlear gene–gene interactions with pathway, cell-type, and experimental context. IEKB further includes a Bayesian “dark matter” module that prioritises 243,071 candidate gene–phenotype associations for 13,229 genes across all 43 phenotypes (global AUC-ROC = 0.8603; global AUC-PR = 0.1674), together with a supervised dark-relation layer that ranks phenotype-specific known-gene support for each candidate and a multi-entity scientific network containing nearly 4,000 entities, 28,616 deterministic edges, and 83,712 literature-derived relational links. The web resource supports interactive search, multi-parameter filtering, gene-detail pages, bibliometric exploration, domain-specific enrichment against IEKB phenotype and disease gene sets, network visualisation, bulk download in CSV, JSON, SQLite, and XLSX formats, and natural-language evidence-grounded question answering through a companion conversational interface (IEKB QA). To our knowledge, IEKB is the first openly accessible inner-ear resource that integrates curated associations, cochlear interactions, probabilistic candidate prioritisation, auditable known-gene support relations for novel candidates, and a multi-entity scientific network within a single database. All data are released without registration under the CC BY 4.0 license.
